Reviewer #1:

The authors present a mathematical model with the ability to generate grid cells, as well as place cells. In this model, each neuron receives excitatory and inhibitory input, which can exhibit varying degrees of smoothness across space. The neural activity evolves according to classic Hebbian plasticity rules, and the relationship between the smoothness of the excitatory versus inhibitory input dictates whether a place field, grid fields, or no spatial tuning at all, is exhibited by the neuron after learning. The authors showed that this model can learn somewhat rapidly, and extended their results to include head direction tuning as well. I think while it is quite bold to present a non-attractor network model of grid cells, especially when there's a lot of evidence that point to grid cells as an attractor network (e.g. Yoon et al., 2013), this model is also interesting and may help explain some of the other non-grid spatial patterns, and conjunctive coding, found in MEC and other parahippocampal areas. The paper is also clear, well-presented, and appears to be very transparent, which is appreciated. However, I think this paper could be further improved by comparing to experimental results, and by fully detailing the caveats and differences with the attractor network model.

1) I don't know if this is possible, but it would be nice if the authors could connect more of the predictions of the model back to data. For example, the authors show that in their conjunctive grid-head direction cells, the head direction preference is also a function of location. The authors state that whether or not this is the case is the data is 'unresolved', but it would be really nice if the authors could dig into this a bit further. This is another prediction that could potentially allow the field to distinguish between this model and the attractor network, and with the amount of grid cell data that is publicly available, it seems possible to at least demonstrate what is currently known.

2) Additionally, it is not completely clear what bells and whistles would have to be added to this model to reproduce the experimental results that the attractor network captures (e.g. that nearby grid cells have a similar orientation and spacing, and may preferentially functionally connect to each other (Dunn et al., 2015)). The authors should expand upon this part so the two models can be compared on a more equal footing.

3) The timescale of learning seems to be a bit of an issue to me. I appreciate that this model does better than others, but I still think that this part of the paper could be expanded upon a bit. When an animal is in a novel environment, the grid pattern appears to be there almost immediately (Hafting et al., 2005). Perhaps this is difficult to actually see, since the animal needs to cover the environment at least once over to see a robust grid pattern. It might be nice to see some examples of what the firing pattern would look like after 3-5 minutes of exploration (perhaps with behavioral trajectories from the Sargolini data), so the model can be mapped directly back to what has been observed experimentally.

Alternatively – I suppose one way around this is that the spatial inputs to the cell don't change with environment, but then this input can't be place cells, which can remap across environments. Perhaps another alternative is that the input comes from non-grid spatial cells in MEC, although these also might not be stable enough across environments (Diehl et al., 2017). Have the authors considered whether the inputs do (or don't) change across environments, and what that might do the stability of the grid pattern?

4) It is a little unclear to me what the spatial inputs are – biologically speaking – to the place cells. The authors state that this is not fully resolved, but I think this should be fleshed out a bit more, given that the entire basis of the model is on these cell types. The input to the grid cells (combinations of place cell, or place cell like cells) seems a bit more grounded, but the authors should expand upon what the inputs to the place cells might actually be. Otherwise, in some parts of the paper, it seems a bit like a place cell is generated from the combined inputs of other place cells (which could also be true, but then as presented feels a bit circular and not as exciting or novel).

5) Is it possible to get non-grid spatial cells, and non-grid spatial cells that also encode head direction and/or running speed, like that seen in Deihl et al., 2017?

Reviewer #2:

This paper presents a neural network model of the development of the spatial tunings of different cell types in the hippocampal formation, with special emphasis on grid cells. The authors use rate-based excitatory and inhibitory neurons, in conjunction with simple learning rules, to show that based on the relative smoothness of the spatial profiles of the inhibitory and excitatory inputs, the same learning rule can yield grid-like, place-like, or spatially invariant tunings in the output neurons. In particular, grid cell period is determined by the width of the inhibitory inputs, as shown through simulation and analytics. The authors demonstrate their finding using both simplistic unimodal spatial inputs as well as more realistic non-local, multimodal inputs.

I found the paper to be easy to understand, in particular because the learning rules (Hebbian excitatory and homeostatic Hebbian inhibitory) are straightforward, and their effects on the self-organization of the overall tuning by the rearrangement of activity clusters is intuitive and well described. Further, I found the extension of the model to non-local inputs to be an important result, as too often overly simplistic inputs are used for training. I have a few major comments:

1) As the authors point out, it is well known that grids belonging to the same module share a similar orientation, and that this is an issue for single-cell feedforward models. The authors cite Si et al., 2012 as a potential mechanism for orienting the grids, who show that grid formation and alignment emerge simultaneously. Given that a major thrust of the paper is to show that grids can be learned on the time scale at which they are experimentally ascertained, and therefore that the learning rule is biologically plausible, it is incumbent on the authors to demonstrate that learning to align the grids will not interfere with grid self-organization as proposed in their model, and that it is possible to do so within a reasonable time frame. A supplementary figure should be sufficient.

2) Along similar lines, the authors criticize continuous attractor network (CAN) developmental models of grid cells (in particular, Widloski and Fiete 2014) for their slowness of learning. The authors miss the point here, for while in these models grids are slow to develop during exposure to the first environment, during which the recurrent weights develop (trained on unimodal spatial inputs similar to those used in the author's work), they are rapidly expressed in any other environment afterwards, unfamiliar or not. This is because, once the continuous attractor is established (and this only needs to be done once), grid field expression is simply a matter of network path integration. Thus, grids appear instantly, even in the absence of localized information (e.g., darkness), and shared grid orientation comes for free.

3) In Figure 3—figure supplement 3, the author's state that "early firing fields are still present in the final grid", and say that this is consistent with Hafting et al., 2005. In this figure, the considerable drift in the fields over time makes it hard to relate fields expressed at the end of learning with those at the beginning. I would like to see this quantified in some way other than gridness score, maybe through measuring rate map correlations between the final mature map and the map as it develops in time. To what extent is there phase/scale/orientation drift through time? Further, it is interesting that, according to Figure 3C, the gridness develops rather abruptly, consistent with papers from Wills et al., (Wills et al., 2010, 2012). Does phase/scale/orientation also develop/stabilize with a similar time course?

4) The distinction between feedforward models (for example in this paper) and CAN models is clear, but less so between different feed forward models that self-organize in similar ways. I would like to see these fleshed out a bit more in the Discussion, in particular with regards to Castro and Aguiar, 2014 and Stepanyuk, 2015, as many might not be aware of them.

5) It is well known that grid cells recorded in 1d exhibit tuning curves that are strikingly non-periodic. Recently, it was shown (Yoon et al., 2016) that for cells belonging to the same module, these 1d responses are consistent with slices through the same 2d lattice. The authors propose a model that can potentially develop aperiodic grids when using non-local inputs. However, getting the right aperiodicities across cells so that they correspond to slices through the same 2d lattice would seem difficult.

Reviewer #3:

This study proposes a general mechanism for the emergence of the diverse spatial correlates found in the hippocampal formation. Through formal analysis and computational simulations, the authors show that the firing patterns of place cells, grid cells, head direction cells, and related conjunctive correlates can all be obtained by particular forms of synaptic plasticity operating on spatially modulated, excitatory and inhibitory inputs. This framework is interesting for at least two reasons. First, it offers insights that complement those derived from models based on path integration, especially in regard to the sensory-dependent characteristics of these correlates. Second, it suggests a specific role for inhibitory inputs and circuits, which have received increasing attention in the context of the entorhinal cortical architecture and grid cells. Below I summarize my main concerns before providing more detailed comments.

The success of this model appears to rest on the ad hoc design of spatial inputs (both excitatory and inhibitory) that often seem unrealistic, combined with equally ad hoc choices for the learning rates of the synaptic plasticity operating on these inputs (examples discussed below). Moreover, while I appreciate the theoretical appeal of reducing the emergence of the many diverse types of spatial correlates to a single unifying mechanism, this approach is very likely to overlook the functional significance of the complex and varied architecture of the circuits of the hippocampal formation, and to oversimplify the computational interaction of the spatial correlates in these circuits. Thus the proposed framework seems to shift the complexity of the spatial tunings that it aims to explain one synapse upstream, by assuming a perplexing and yet undocumented degree of specificity and organization in the modulation of inhibitory input patterns and their plasticity.

As to the organization of the paper, the mathematical analysis that is described in the Materials and methods section appears an important part of the results in this study. Checking all the mathematical derivations thoroughly is a task better fitting the peer-review style and timeframe of more theoretically oriented journals, and I have only read this part superficially. Still, I think that a summary of the main results of this analysis should be included in the Results section and accompanied by an intuitive explanation. Full derivations should still be provided separately (as they are now, but possibly in an appendix, rather than in the Materials and methods section – again this is because I see the mathematical analysis as one of the contributions/results of this paper, rather than a method). I think such a reorganization would benefit the dissemination of the complete results of this paper to a general audience.

results.result: Neurons in the hippocampus and adjacent brain areas show diverse spatial tuning patterns, with certain cell types being selective to one spatial variable but invariant to another (e.g., place cells are typically invariant to head direction). The underlying circuit mechanisms for this diversity are not yet resolved.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 accurately describe established knowledge in the field regarding spatial tuning diversity in hippocampal neurons and the open questions about underlying mechanisms. These are well-documented observations supported by the cited literature (C10-C14) and represent the scientific context motivating the study.

results.result: The authors propose that all observed spatial tuning patterns arise from a common mechanism: excitatory and inhibitory synaptic plasticity driven by the spatial tuning statistics of synaptic inputs, with differences in response profiles resulting from differences in the spatial tuning of excitatory and inhibitory afferents.
results.evaluation: This is the central hypothesis of the paper (C5, C18, C19). While these are speculative claims about the mechanism, they are supported by the extensive simulation results (C6, C7, C20) and mathematical analysis presented throughout the manuscript. The model successfully reproduces diverse spatial tuning patterns as demonstrated in multiple figures.

results.result: Combined excitatory and inhibitory plasticity can lead to localized, grid-like, or invariant activity patterns. The model reproduces all major spatial tuning patterns observed in rodents, with the relative spatial smoothness of inhibitory and excitatory input determining the symmetry of the spatial firing pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C20, C46, C62, and C86 are strongly supported by simulation results shown throughout the paper (Figures 1-6). The mathematical analysis and multiple simulation scenarios with different input statistics consistently demonstrate that the model can produce the diverse spatial tuning patterns observed experimentally.

results.result: The mechanism by which different spatial patterns emerge depends on the relative smoothness of excitatory and inhibitory input tuning. Smoother inhibitory tuning leads to grid-like patterns through the formation of inhibitory coronas, while smoother excitatory tuning leads to spatial invariance. Spatially untuned inhibition produces single place fields.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C41 describe the core mechanistic explanation for pattern formation, supported by simulations in Figure 1 and mathematical analysis. The explanation of inhibitory coronas and their role in creating periodic patterns is clearly demonstrated and theoretically justified. The mechanism is consistent across different input types.

results.result: The width of individual firing fields is determined by the smoothness of excitatory input tuning, while grid spacing is set by the smoothness of inhibitory input tuning. Grid spacing scales linearly with inhibitory smoothness and has a weak logarithmic dependence on the ratio of learning rates, mean firing rates, and number of afferents.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are supported by both simulations (Figures 1g, 1h) and mathematical analysis (Equation 78, Figure 8b). The linear relationship between grid spacing and inhibitory smoothness is clearly demonstrated, and the mathematical derivation provides theoretical justification for the observed relationships.

results.result: In two-dimensional arenas, the model produces hexagonal grid patterns similar to those observed in medial entorhinal cortex. The hexagonal arrangement results from smoother inhibitory input tuning generating spherical inhibitory coronas, with spacing determined by inhibitory smoothness.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C53 are supported by simulations in Figure 2 and comparison with experimental observations (C47 cites Hafting et al., 2005; Fyhn et al., 2004). The emergence of hexagonal patterns from the model is clearly demonstrated, and the geometric explanation (closest packing of spheres) is well-justified.

results.result: For different input types (place cell-like, sparse non-localized, dense non-localized), the model produces grid-like patterns with varying degrees of distortion. The fraction of cells with positive grid scores increases substantially after learning (33-35% to 68-87%), with less distortion for sparser input.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59, C63 are quantitatively supported by the grid score histograms in Figure 2d-f and the analysis in Figure 2g. The model successfully produces grid patterns across different input types, though with varying quality. The observation that sparser input produces less distorted grids is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: The model is robust to parameter changes and develops patterns on behavioral timescales. Periodic patterns can be discerned within 10 minutes of spatial exploration, with hexagonal symmetry emerging within hours. In 500 realizations, periodic patterns emerged within 30 minutes in all simulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C9, C66-C69, C77, C142 are strongly supported by the time-course simulations in Figure 3. The rapid emergence of patterns (within minutes to hours) is clearly demonstrated across multiple realizations, addressing a key challenge for plasticity-based models. The robustness is shown through 500 different realizations with varied parameters.

results.result: The output firing pattern is robust to perturbations, remaining stable even when more than half of the inputs are remapped. When all inputs are changed (novel room), a new grid pattern is learned without hindrance from the previous weight pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73 are supported by simulations in Figure 3—figure supplement 2. The model demonstrates appropriate robustness to partial input remapping while still being able to learn new patterns when inputs are completely changed, which is consistent with experimental observations of grid cell behavior in different environments.

results.result: The model reproduces the experimental observation that grid cells form independent patterns on each side of a partition wall that coalesce when the wall is removed, with grid fields close to the partition rearranging while distant fields remain stable.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76 are supported by simulations in Figure 4 and comparison with recent experimental findings (Wernle et al., 2018). The model successfully reproduces the local rearrangement of grid fields near the partition wall while maintaining stability of distant fields, demonstrating its ability to capture complex spatial dynamics.

results.result: The model produces place cells, band cells, and stretched grids by varying the spatial smoothness of inhibitory inputs along different dimensions. Place cells emerge from very smooth inhibitory input, band cells from asymmetric smoothness, and stretched grids from anisotropic but smoother inhibition. The requirements for invariance, periodicity, and localization apply individually to each spatial dimension.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C85, C87 are supported by simulations in Figure 5. The model demonstrates remarkable flexibility in producing diverse spatial tuning patterns by varying input statistics along different dimensions. The mechanistic explanation for different pattern types (dense packing vs. maximizing excitatory overlap) is well-reasoned.

results.result: The model extends to head direction tuning, with the relative smoothness of inhibitory and excitatory inputs in both space and head direction determining whether the output cell fires like a pure grid cell, conjunctive cell, or pure head direction cell.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C98 are supported by simulations in Figure 6. The model successfully extends the same principles to head direction tuning, producing grid cells, conjunctive cells, and head direction cells depending on the relative smoothness of inputs in spatial and head direction dimensions. This demonstrates the generality of the proposed mechanism.

results.result: In conjunctive cells, the overall head direction tuning is broader than that of individual grid fields due to variations in preferred head direction across different grid fields, though individual fields tend to align their head direction tuning.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 are supported by simulations in Figure 6e. The model makes a specific prediction about the relationship between overall and field-specific head direction tuning in conjunctive cells. However, the authors acknowledge that experimental validation of this prediction requires additional data (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).

results.result: The main prediction of the model is that the spatial autocorrelation structure of excitatory and inhibitory inputs determines and should be predictable from the output pattern of the cell. Investigations of the tuning of individual cells or synapses projecting to spatially tuned cells would be a litmus test for the proposed mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 clearly state the key experimental prediction of the model. This is a logical consequence of the model's structure and is appropriately identified as the primary testable prediction. The suggestion of specific experimental approaches (Wertz et al., 2015; Wilson et al., 2016) is well-supported by citations to relevant techniques.

results.result: In contrast to CAN models where inhibition reduction changes grid spacing, the proposed model predicts that rapid global reduction of inhibition changes only grid field size, not locations. This prediction is consistent with experimental observations that grid spacing remains constant during inhibitory interneuron silencing.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C125 are supported by simulations in Figure 7a and comparison with experimental data (Miao et al., 2017; Cilz et al., 2014). This represents a clear distinguishing prediction between the proposed model and CAN models, with experimental support for the model's prediction.

results.result: For localized input tuning, the inhibitory membrane current peaks at grid field locations, but this co-tuning breaks down for non-localized input. This differs from CAN model predictions of periodic inhibitory current with the same periodicity as the grid.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C128 are supported by simulations in Figure 7b,c. The model makes a specific prediction about inhibitory membrane currents that differs from CAN models and depends on input type. This provides another distinguishing experimental test between model classes.

results.result: The similarity between cells in terms of grid orientation and phase depends on whether they receive the same inputs, on the trajectories during learning, and on initial synaptic weights. Two grid cells can have different phase and orientation even if they share most or all inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 are supported by simulations in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The model provides insight into factors determining grid cell coordination, though the authors acknowledge that additional mechanisms may be needed for full coordination of neighboring grid cells (C132-C133).

results.result: The model architecture consists of a single output neuron receiving feedforward input from excitatory and inhibitory neurons with spatially tuned, temporally stable firing rates. Excitatory weights follow Hebbian plasticity, while inhibitory weights follow homeostatic plasticity that balances excitation and inhibition to maintain a target firing rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C30 describe the model architecture and plasticity rules. These are clearly specified in the text and Materials and Methods. The inhibitory plasticity rule is supported by previous work (C29 cites Vogels et al., 2011; D'Amour and Froemke, 2015). The assumption of fast inhibitory plasticity (C30) is reasonable but should be noted as a model assumption.

results.result: The model is consistent with multiple potential sources of spatially tuned input, including higher sensory areas, hippocampal place cells, and local entorhinal interneurons. Several lines of anatomical and functional evidence support these potential input sources, including developmental timing, lesion studies, and anatomical connectivity patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C120 discuss potential input sources and their consistency with the model. These are appropriately presented as speculative (C105) but are well-supported by extensive citations to anatomical and functional studies. The discussion appropriately acknowledges that input sources are not fully resolved (C104) while showing the model is consistent with multiple possibilities.

results.result: The proposed model differs from other plasticity-based models by relying on spatial rather than temporal statistics of input, enabling faster pattern formation. Unlike CAN models that would show immediate grid patterns once connectivity is established, the proposed model shows rapid but not instantaneous emergence of patterns in new environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C148 compare the proposed model to other approaches. The comparisons are well-supported by citations and simulation results (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). The key distinction—reliance on spatial vs. temporal statistics—is clearly articulated and has important implications for pattern formation speed.

results.result: The model can explain local rearrangement of grid fields and shows boundary effects on grid patterns. Simulations show that boundaries distort grid patterns, particularly for localized inputs, consistent with experimental observations in different arena geometries.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C153 are supported by simulations in Figure 4 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3. The model demonstrates appropriate sensitivity to environmental geometry, though the authors note that pronounced alignment to boundaries requires specific input configurations.

results.result: The interaction of excitatory and inhibitory plasticity serves as a simple and robust mechanism for rapid self-organization of stable and symmetric patterns from spatially modulated feedforward input. This mechanism may be essential for forming stable representations from sensory input in other brain areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C156 summarize the main conclusions and are well-supported by the extensive simulation and analytical results presented throughout the paper. Claim C157 is appropriately speculative about broader implications, supported by citations to relevant work in other brain areas (Constantinescu et al., 2016; Clopath et al., 2016).

results.result: The model differs from existing approaches (CAN models and other single-cell models) in several key predictions and requirements. CAN models predict coordinated grid cells and uniform head direction tuning across grid fields, while single-cell models require additional mechanisms for coordination. The proposed model makes distinct predictions about head direction tuning variability across grid fields.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C17, C129-C137 provide context about existing models and distinguish the proposed approach. These comparisons are well-supported by citations and clearly articulate the differences in predictions and requirements between model classes. The distinctions provide testable hypotheses for future experiments.
